title: The moths and the lamp
hook: insects flying into the oil lamps at night

segments.voice: Yesterday: the elephant, read whole. Your line: listen to the whole. Today, a scene in the Udana that's over in a few lines.

A porch light on a summer night. Moths come out of the dark, circle the bulb, bump it, drift off, circle again. A bulb is one thing. An open flame is another: a moth that flies into a candle or an oil lamp doesn't come out again. Why do they keep coming? The Udana doesn't try to explain the moths. It just watches them.
screen: `A PORCH LIGHT ON A SUMMER NIGHT.` → `A FLAME IS DIFFERENT.` → `THE UDANA JUST WATCHES.`

segments.voice: The whole story takes a few lines. The Buddha is sitting outdoors in the dark of the night, and oil lamps are burning. Winged insects are flying around them and falling in, one after another, to their harm, to their ruin. The Buddha sees this, and, knowing the meaning of it, speaks a verse. Rushing up, passing by what's essential, they bring on new bonds again and again, like insects falling into a lamp. So some are bound up in what is seen and heard. That's all. No crowd, no question, no long teaching. A man sitting in the dark, watching. Notice the phrase in the middle: passing by what's essential. The moths aren't stupid. They're drawn by something real, the light. The trouble is that they mistake it for something it isn't, and keep coming back. The verse says people can do the same with the seen and the heard: the bright thing on the screen, the voice that pulls at us, each rush tying another knot. There's a link back to Bahiya, a few days ago: in the seen, only the seen. The moth doesn't stop at the seen. It flies straight in. And the Buddha doesn't put out the lamps or explain the insects. He sits in the dark, sees them, and speaks about people.
screen: `OIL LAMPS BURNING IN THE DARK.` · `FALLING IN, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `PASSING BY WHAT'S ESSENTIAL.` · `BOUND BY THE SEEN AND THE HEARD.` · then, large: `THE MOTHS AND THE FLAME.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what bright thing you keep circling, even when it burns a little: a feed, a fight, a craving, an evening that always ends the same way. Picture it as a lamp in the dark, and watch yourself circling it with kindness, the way the Buddha watched the moths. You don't have to stop yet; just see the circling.
Adhipataka, a moth. In the Udana, insects falling into oil lamps at night: the picture of rushing again and again to the seen and the heard. Today's word.
Your line: the moths and the flame. The light is real; the rushing is the trouble. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes use the image of insects and a flame for craving that harms the one who craves, drawing on scenes like this one in the Udana.

original.note: Pali adhipataka: a moth or winged insect. in Udana 6.9 they fall into the oil lamps.

trapdoor: what you thought: moths are drawn to light because they're foolish.
what it means: they're drawn by something real, and mistake it; the verse says people do the same with the seen and the heard.

what a scholar hears: Udana 6.9 calls the insects adhipataka, and its verse says they rush past and never reach the core (na saram enti), binding on new bonds again and again, settled in the seen and heard.

chat.says: What's the point of that Buddhist scene with the moths and the lamps?
options: People can rush again and again at what they see and hear, like moths.
It teaches that moths are foolish creatures with no sense of their own.
It warns that lamps do harm, so they should be put out every night.
chat.meaning: In Udana 6.9 the verse compares people bound up in the seen and the heard to insects falling into a lamp, again and again.
